name: SBI PO
fullName: State Bank of India – Probationary Officers Recruitment
conductingBody: State Bank of India (Central Recruitment & Promotion Department)
eligibility: Graduate in any discipline (final-year students may apply provisionally); 21–30 years (relaxation for reserved categories)

notification.summary: SBI PO 2026 (Advt. CRPD/PO/2026-27/09) is in progress: prelims were held on 1–2 Aug 2026, the prelims result was declared on 28 Aug 2026 and the mains was held on 12 Sep 2026; Phase III (psychometric test, group exercise and interview) is next. Reports mention ≈1,500 vacancies. Dates are from news portals; SBI's careers page could not be opened from the research environment.

pattern.notes: 20 minutes per section with separate timers. No sectional cut-off in recent SBI PO prelims (overall, category-wise cut-off; about 10× vacancies shortlisted). Prelims is qualifying only. Phase II mains (objective + descriptive) and Phase III (psychometric test, group exercise, interview) follow.

trendAnalysis.summary: SBI PO prelims has been easy-to-moderate in English and moderate in Quant and Reasoning; good attempts were ≈66–74 in Aug 2026. English (40 Qs) relies on RC (≈7–10), cloze (5–6), rearrangement/para-jumble (5), double fillers, word swap and error spotting, with new formats such as column-based sentence matching. Quant is DI-heavy (2–3 sets incl. caselets and missing-data tables) with quadratic/quantity-comparison, number series and arithmetic word problems. Reasoning is dominated by puzzles and seating arrangements (≈15–18 Qs: parallel-row, floor-flat, month/year puzzles) plus syllogism, inequality and quick misc questions (meaningful words, pairs).

pyqBlueprint.method: Compiled from shift-wise memory-based analyses of SBI PO prelims of the 2024 notification (exam held March 2025) and the 2025 notification (exam held August 2025) published by coaching sites (Physics Wallah, Adda247, Career Power, Edutap), cross-checked with the official SBI prelims pattern (40 English, 30 Quant, 30 Reasoning). A detailed 2026 analysis was not available, so archetypes are backed by 2024 and 2025. Patterns are paraphrased; no real question is reproduced.

archetypes.pattern: RC set (350–450 words, economy/banking/technology/environment theme): identify the central idea or main argument; distractors are true-but-partial details or over-generalisations
RC fact-check: 'Which of the following is true / NOT true according to the passage' — one option distorts a qualifier (some→most, may→will) or reverses cause and effect
RC inference with statements I, II, III and combination options (Only I / Only I and III …); the trap statement overstates what the passage says
RC vocabulary-in-context: synonym or antonym of a word used in the passage, with distractors that are dictionary meanings not fitting the context
RC purpose/tone/title: why the author mentions a detail, the author's tone, or the most suitable title
Passage cloze with numbered blanks; five same-part-of-speech options where distractors are look-alike or collocation-breaking words
Cloze with a bold word already in each blank: choose the correct replacement or 'No replacement required'
Sentence split into parts (A)–(D) plus 'No error' (E); errors in subject–verb agreement, prepositions, pronouns, tense, comparatives, or inversion after negative adverbs
Choose the grammatically correct (or incorrect) sentence among five similar sentences on one theme
Double filler: two blanks in one sentence, five word-pairs where one word of each wrong pair fits but the other does not
Single filler: one blank, five words close in meaning; only one matches the tone/collocation of the sentence
Para jumble of five or six sentences on one theme; choose the correct order (options are sequences); connectors like 'however', 'as a result' and pronouns fix the order
Para jumble asking which sentence comes FIRST / THIRD / LAST after rearrangement (options are sentence letters)
Sentence rearrangement: order four fragments (P, Q, R, S) into one grammatically correct sentence
Word swap: four highlighted words in a sentence; identify the pair whose interchange makes the sentence correct, or 'No interchange required'
Word usage: one word used in three sentences (I, II, III); identify in which sentence(s) it is used correctly
Phrase replacement: a highlighted phrase with a grammar/idiom error; choose the correct replacement, or 'No replacement required'
Standalone synonym/antonym of a moderately advanced word; distractors include words of the opposite sense
Connector: choose the word/phrase that joins two sentences without changing the meaning (cause, contrast, condition)
Column-based: match sentence halves from Column I and Column II; options list the meaningful combinations
Table DI (5 rows × 2–3 columns): percentage increase/decrease of one entity between two years, or one entity as a percentage of another
Table DI with a percentage column (e.g. share of a sub-category): compute derived values (sum, average, difference or ratio of derived quantities)
Caselet DI: a paragraph giving a total and splits in ratios/percentages; questions combine two splits or ask what changes after a transfer
Pie-chart DI (shares in % or degrees of a total): find values, differences and ratios across sectors
Two quadratic equations in x and y with integer/fraction roots; compare x and y using the five standard relations (> ≥ < ≤ / cannot be established)
Quantity comparison: Quantity I and Quantity II from two short arithmetic problems or equations; choose the relation
Missing number series built on differences of squares/cubes, alternate ×n +k, or ×n with increasing n
Wrong number series: one term breaks the ×/+ pattern; find it
Profit & loss with marked price, discount and cost price (single or successive discounts, 'had he sold for ₹x more')
Percentage word problem: income–expenditure–savings, successive percentage change, or one value as a percentage of another
Partnership with unequal times or a mid-year change of capital; find a partner's share of profit
Ages: present-age ratio with a condition some years before/after; find an age or sum of ages
Ratio & proportion: dividing an amount in a ratio, or changing a ratio by adding/removing a quantity
Time & work / pipes: efficiencies combined, one leaves after some days, or an emptying pipe
Trains crossing poles/platforms/each other, relative speed, or average speed of a round trip
Boats and streams: downstream/upstream speeds and times
Simple vs compound interest: CI–SI difference, amount at CI, or a sum split between two rates
Mixture & alligation: mixing two varieties to a target price/ratio, or adding/replacing liquid
Probability with balls/cards/committees, using combinations
Mensuration: rectangle/circle/cylinder area, perimeter or volume relationships
Linear row or two parallel rows (8–12 persons) with an attribute; questions on facing person, ends and 'how many between'
Linear arrangement with mixed directions (some face north, some south) or two parallel rows facing each other
Circular table (6–8 persons) facing the centre (or some outside); left/right relations and 'second to the left of' questions
Floor-based puzzle (5–8 floors, sometimes two flats per floor) with a second attribute such as colour/city/fruit
Scheduling puzzle: persons/events on days of the week or months (sometimes with dates 1xth/2xth); 'how many between' questions
Box stacking: boxes placed one above another, with colour/item attribute and 'how many boxes between' clues
Comparison puzzle on heights/weights/ages with 'more than only' clues, sometimes with one numeric value; find rank or a possible value
Syllogism with 2–3 statements and two conclusions, including 'possibility' conclusions; standard five options
Syllogism with 'Only a few' or 'No' statements where a definite 'All' conclusion is the trap
Direct inequality: two or three combined statements, two conclusions to check
Inequality where the conclusions form a complementary pair (A > B / A = B) and the answer is 'Either I or II follows'
Blood relation chain or 'pointing to a photograph' statement; gender ambiguity is the usual trap
Direction & distance: a person walks a path with left/right turns; find the shortest distance and direction from start
Point-based direction: several points given relative to each other; find direction/distance between two of them
Letter coding: word coded by letter shifts / reversal / opposite letters; code a new word
Sentence (Chinese) coding: three or four phrases coded in two-letter codes; find the code of a word by elimination
Order & ranking: positions from both ends of a row/class, total count, or persons between two people
Letter pairs in a word with as many letters between them as in the English alphabet
Meaningful words formed from given letters of a word (each letter used once)

resources.notes: SBI does not publish full PO question papers or answer keys. Official material: the detailed advertisement with exam pattern, and pre-examination training (PET) material for eligible reserved-category candidates on sbi.bank.in/web/careers; candidates can view their own marks after the final result. Previous papers available online are memory-based compilations by coaching institutes.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

The rapid growth of platform-based work has blurred the line between employees and independent contractors. Delivery riders and ride-hailing drivers enjoy flexible hours, but they usually lack the health cover, paid leave and pension contributions that salaried workers take for granted. Platforms argue that classifying these workers as employees would raise costs and reduce the flexibility that many of them value. Labour advocates counter that flexibility is meaningless if a single accident can push a worker's family into debt. A middle path is now emerging in several countries: platforms contribute a small percentage of each transaction to a social-security fund, while workers retain the freedom to log in and out as they wish. Whether such schemes succeed will depend on how accurately earnings are recorded and how easily workers can claim benefits, since a fund that is hard to access offers little real protection.

Which of the following best captures the main idea of the passage?
options: Platform work should be banned because it is unsafe
The debate over social security for platform workers and a possible middle path
How platforms calculate their delivery charges
Labour advocates' opposition to flexible hours
questions.explanation: The passage presents both sides of the classification debate and then describes the emerging contribution-based middle path.

questions.question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
A. Instead, it was the steady rise in the number of small investors.
B. The stock market rally surprised many analysts this year.
C. Most had expected foreign investors to drive the gains.
D. Monthly SIP inflows, in particular, reached record levels.
E. Foreign funds, however, were net sellers for much of the period.
questions.explanation: B (rally surprised analysts) → C (they expected foreign investors) → E (however, foreigners sold) → A (instead, small investors) → D (SIP inflows in particular): BCEAD.

questions.question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph and choose the FIRST sentence.
A. This means a borrower's EMI changes soon after a policy rate change.
B. Many home loans in India are now linked to an external benchmark.
C. Borrowers should therefore track policy announcements closely.
D. The most common benchmark is the central bank's repo rate.
E. Earlier, banks could delay passing on rate cuts to customers.
questions.explanation: B introduces external-benchmark loans; D names the benchmark; A gives the effect; E contrasts with the past; C concludes. The first sentence is B.

The regulator has ______ banks to strengthen their cyber-security systems, as the number of online frauds continues to ______.

A college has 1,600 students: 45% study Commerce, 35% Science and the rest Arts. 60% of Commerce students, 40% of Science students and 25% of Arts students are girls.

What is the total number of boys in the college?
questions.explanation: Commerce 720 (boys 40% = 288), Science 560 (boys 60% = 336), Arts 320 (boys 75% = 240). Total = 864.

questions.question:
A college has 1,600 students: 45% study Commerce, 35% Science and the rest Arts. 60% of Commerce students, 40% of Science students and 25% of Arts students are girls.

The number of girls in Science is what percent of the number of boys in Arts?
questions.explanation: Girls in Science = 40% of 560 = 224; boys in Arts = 75% of 320 = 240. 224/240 × 100 = 93⅓%.

questions.question:
A college has 1,600 students: 45% study Commerce, 35% Science and the rest Arts. 60% of Commerce students, 40% of Science students and 25% of Arts students are girls.

If 25% of the boys in Commerce move to Arts, what will be the ratio of girls to boys in Arts?
questions.explanation: Commerce boys = 288; 25% = 72 move. Arts boys = 240 + 72 = 312, girls = 80. Ratio 80 : 312 = 10 : 39.

questions.question:
Solve and compare.
I. x² + 3x − 40 = 0
II. y² − 13y + 40 = 0
options: x = y or the relationship cannot be established
questions.explanation: I: (x + 8)(x − 5) = 0 → x = −8, 5. II: (y − 5)(y − 8) = 0 → y = 5, 8. Every x is less than or equal to every y (5 = 5), so x ≤ y.

Eight persons sit in two parallel rows of four each. In Row 1, P, Q, R and S sit facing south; in Row 2, A, B, C and D sit facing north, so that each person faces exactly one person of the other row. P faces A. R sits at an extreme end of his row. Only one person sits between R and S. B sits second to the right of A. The person who faces S sits immediately to the left of B. Neither C nor P sits at an extreme end of the row.

Who faces Q?
questions.explanation: Columns from west to east — Row 1 (facing south): R, P, S, Q; Row 2 (facing north): D, A, C, B. Q faces B.

questions.question:
Eight persons sit in two parallel rows of four each. In Row 1, P, Q, R and S sit facing south; in Row 2, A, B, C and D sit facing north, so that each person faces exactly one person of the other row. P faces A. R sits at an extreme end of his row. Only one person sits between R and S. B sits second to the right of A. The person who faces S sits immediately to the left of B. Neither C nor P sits at an extreme end of the row.

Who sits immediately to the right of P?
questions.explanation: Row 1 faces south, so a person's right is towards the west. Row 1 west→east: R, P, S, Q. R is immediately to the right of P.

questions.question:

Which two persons sit at the extreme ends of Row 2?
questions.explanation: Working through the clues: Row 1 (west→east) R, P, S, Q and Row 2 (west→east) D, A, C, B. D and B sit at the ends of Row 2.

questions.question:
Seven persons L, M, N, O, P, Q and R have birthdays in seven different months of the same year — January, March, April, June, August, October and December (in calendar order; 'immediately before' refers to these seven months only). L's birthday is in a month that has 30 days. Only two persons have birthdays between L and Q. M's birthday is immediately before Q's. O's birthday is after Q's. R's birthday is immediately before M's. N's birthday is before P's. Neither N nor P has a birthday in a month that has 30 days.

Whose birthday is in June?
questions.explanation: Order: N (Jan), P (Mar), L (Apr), R (Jun), M (Aug), Q (Oct), O (Dec). R's birthday is in June.

questions.question:

R's birthday is immediately before M's. N's birthday is before P's. Neither N nor P has a birthday in a month that has 30 days.

How many persons have birthdays between N and M?
questions.explanation: Order: N (Jan), P (Mar), L (Apr), R (Jun), M (Aug), Q (Oct), O (Dec). Between N and M: P, L and R — three.

questions.question:
Seven persons L, M, N, O, P, Q and R have birthdays in seven different months of the same year — January, March, April, June, August, October and December (in calendar order; 'immediately before' refers to these seven months only). L's birthday is in a month that has 30 days. Only two persons have birthdays between L and Q. M's birthday is immediately before Q's. O's birthday is after Q's. R's birthday is immediately before M's. N's birthday is before P's. Neither N nor P has a birthday in a month that has 30 days.

In which month is Q's birthday?
questions.explanation: L must be Apr or Jun; with two persons between L and Q, and R, M, Q consecutive with O after Q, only L = Apr, R = Jun, M = Aug, Q = Oct, O = Dec works. N and P take Jan and Mar. Q's birthday is in October.

questions.question:
Eight persons J, T, U, V, W, X, Y and Z live in a four-storey building (floor 1 is the bottom, floor 4 the top). Each floor has two flats — West and East — with one person in each flat. T lives in an East flat on an even-numbered floor. Z lives in the flat immediately below T's flat (same side, one floor lower). V lives on the same floor as Z. Y lives in a West flat on a floor below J's floor. Only one floor lies between U's floor and X's floor, and U lives in an East flat. W lives on floor 1.

Who lives in the West flat of floor 3?
questions.explanation: Floor 4: X (W), T (E); floor 3: V (W), Z (E); floor 2: J (W), U (E); floor 1: Y (W), W (E). V lives in 3-West.

questions.question:
Eight persons J, T, U, V, W, X, Y and Z live in a four-storey building (floor 1 is the bottom, floor 4 the top). Each floor has two flats — West and East — with one person in each flat. T lives in an East flat on an even-numbered floor. Z lives in the flat immediately below T's flat (same side, one floor lower). V lives on the same floor as Z. Y lives in a West flat on a floor below J's floor. Only one floor lies between U's floor and X's floor, and U lives in an East flat. W lives on floor 1.

Who lives on the same floor as U?
questions.explanation: Floor 2 has J (West) and U (East).

questions.question:
Eight persons J, T, U, V, W, X, Y and Z live in a four-storey building (floor 1 is the bottom, floor 4 the top). Each floor has two flats — West and East — with one person in each flat. T lives in an East flat on an even-numbered floor. Z lives in the flat immediately below T's flat (same side, one floor lower). V lives on the same floor as Z. Y lives in a West flat on a floor below J's floor. Only one floor lies between U's floor and X's floor, and U lives in an East flat. W lives on floor 1.

Which of the following statements is true?
options: X lives in the East flat of floor 4
W lives in the West flat of floor 1
questions.explanation: T cannot be in 2-East (Z and V would then fill floor 1, leaving no room for W), so T is 4-East, Z 3-East and V 3-West. U (East) must be 2-East with X on floor 4 (West). W is on floor 1, so Y is 1-West and J 2-West. Y (1-West) lives immediately below J (2-West).

questions.question:
Statements: Some apples are mangoes. All mangoes are grapes. No grape is a lemon.
Conclusions: I. Some apples are not lemons. II. No mango is a lemon.
questions.explanation: Apples that are mangoes are grapes and therefore not lemons (I follows). All mangoes are grapes and no grape is a lemon, so no mango is a lemon (II follows).

questions.question:
Statements: All doctors are nurses. Only a few nurses are teachers. No teacher is a lawyer.
Conclusions: I. Some doctors being teachers is a possibility. II. All nurses can be lawyers.
questions.explanation: Doctors (all nurses) may lie among the nurses who are teachers — I is possible. Some nurses are teachers and no teacher is a lawyer, so those nurses cannot be lawyers — II is false.

questions.question:
Statements: J > K ≥ L; M ≤ L < N; O ≥ M
Conclusions: I. J > M  II. O > K
questions.explanation: J > K ≥ L ≥ M gives J > M. O and K are linked only through M (O ≥ M ≤ L ≤ K), so no relation — only I follows.

questions.question:
Statements: A > B = C ≥ D; E ≤ D < F; G ≥ F
Conclusions: I. C > E  II. C = E
questions.explanation: C ≥ D ≥ E gives C ≥ E. Neither 'C > E' nor 'C = E' is definite alone, but together they cover all cases — either I or II follows.

questions.question: P is the husband of Q. R is the son of P. S is the daughter of Q. T is the wife of R. U is the son of T and R. How is S related to U?
questions.explanation: R and S are children of the couple P–Q, so S is R's sister. U is R's son, so S is U's (paternal) aunt.

questions.question: A man walks 4 km south, turns left and walks 3 km, turns left again and walks 10 km, then turns right and walks 5 km. How far and in which direction is he from his starting point?
questions.explanation: South 4 → left (east) 3 → left (north) 10 → right (east) 5. Net: 8 km east, 6 km north. Distance √(64 + 36) = 10 km, towards the North-East.

questions.question: In a certain code, every consonant is replaced by its position in the English alphabet and every vowel is kept unchanged. 'FOCUS' is written as '6O3U19'. How is 'BASIC' written?
questions.explanation: B = 2, A stays, S = 19, I stays, C = 3 → 2A19I3.

questions.question: Using the 1st, 3rd, 6th and 7th letters of the word 'DIGITAL', exactly how many meaningful English words can be formed? If exactly one, give its third letter; if none, answer X; if more than one, answer Z.
questions.explanation: The letters are D, G, A, L, which form only 'GLAD'. Its third letter is A.

questions.question: Ravi ranks 9th from the top and 26th from the bottom in his class. How many students are in the class?

Read the passage and answer the question.

India is often described as a young country, and for now the description holds. Yet the share of citizens above sixty is rising faster than the population as a whole, and by the middle of the century roughly one in five Indians is expected to be elderly. Unlike many richer nations, India is growing old before it has grown rich. Most workers are employed informally, without an employer who deducts pension contributions, and many reach old age with little more than a small plot of land or the goodwill of their children.

The traditional safety net — the joint family — is fraying. Younger members migrate to cities for work, and smaller households mean fewer hands to share the cost of caring for parents. Women, who on average live longer than men and are less likely to have worked for a wage, are especially exposed.

Voluntary, contribution-based pension schemes have extended coverage to millions, but contributions are often small and irregular, and many subscribers stop paying after a few years. Some economists argue for a modest universal pension financed from taxes; others warn that such a promise could strain public finances as the number of beneficiaries swells. A middle path may lie in matching contributions — where the state adds a sum to every rupee a low-income worker saves — combined with steps to make saving automatic. Whatever the design, the window for preparing is narrowing: a demographic dividend that is not used to build savings today becomes a demographic burden tomorrow.

Which of the following best expresses the central theme of the passage?
options: India is ageing before its incomes are high, so old-age income security must be strengthened while the demographic window is still open
The joint family still guarantees adequate security for India's elderly
A tax-financed universal pension is the only workable solution
Voluntary pension schemes have already achieved near-universal coverage
Migration to cities has made India a young country
questions.explanation: The passage describes rapid ageing amid informal work and a weakening family net, weighs pension designs, and ends by stressing that the window to prepare is narrowing.

Many subscribers to voluntary schemes stop contributing after a few years
The share of people above sixty is growing faster than the overall population

questions.explanation: I follows from 'a demographic dividend that is not used … becomes a demographic burden'. II is how the passage defines matching contributions. III is wrong — 'some economists argue for' a universal pension.

questions.question:
Read the passage and choose the most appropriate option for the numbered blank.

Electric buses are quickly (1) ______ diesel fleets in several Indian cities. Their running costs are lower, and because they produce no exhaust at street level, they also (2) ______ the air that commuters breathe. The bigger hurdle is the high upfront price, which many transport corporations cannot (3) AFFORD on their own; leasing models, in which a private operator owns the bus and is paid per kilometre, have helped bridge this gap.

Which word best fits blank (1)?
questions.explanation: Electric buses are taking the place of diesel fleets — 'replacing'. The other look-alike words do not make sense with 'diesel fleets'.

questions.question:
Read the passage and choose the most appropriate option for the numbered blank.

Electric buses are quickly (1) ______ diesel fleets in several Indian cities. Their running costs are lower, and because they produce no exhaust at street level, they also (2) ______ the air that commuters breathe. The bigger hurdle is the high upfront price, which many transport corporations cannot (3) AFFORD on their own; leasing models, in which a private operator owns the bus and is paid per kilometre, have helped bridge this gap.

Which word best fits blank (2)?
questions.explanation: Because they produce no exhaust, electric buses keep the air cleaner; all other options describe harm.

questions.question:
Read the passage and choose the most appropriate option for the numbered blank.

Electric buses are quickly (1) ______ diesel fleets in several Indian cities. Their running costs are lower, and because they produce no exhaust at street level, they also (2) ______ the air that commuters breathe. The bigger hurdle is the high upfront price, which many transport corporations cannot (3) AFFORD on their own; leasing models, in which a private operator owns the bus and is paid per kilometre, have helped bridge this gap.

The word in capitals at (3) may or may not be correct. Choose the word that should replace it, or choose 'No replacement required'.
questions.explanation: Corporations cannot 'afford' the high upfront price on their own — the word already fits, so no replacement is needed.

questions.question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
A. This shift has forced banks to rethink the role of their branches.
B. A decade ago, most customers visited a branch to deposit cash or update a passbook.
C. Today, the majority of such routine transactions happen on a phone.
D. Many branches are therefore being redesigned as advisory centres for loans and investments.
E. Staff, in turn, are being trained to explain financial products rather than count cash.
questions.explanation: B (past) – C (today, 'such routine transactions') – A ('this shift') – D ('therefore' redesigned) – E ('in turn', staff): BCADE.

questions.question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph and choose the SECOND sentence.
A. Its organisers therefore decided to go plastic-free this year.
B. Vendors were offered steel plates and cups on rent at a nominal fee.
C. Visitors who brought their own bottles got discounts on food.
D. As a result, the waste collected fell by more than half.
E. The town's annual food festival used to leave the grounds littered with plastic.
questions.explanation: E introduces the problem, A ('Its organisers therefore') responds to it, B and C describe the measures and D gives the result. The second sentence is A.

questions.question:
Rearrange the parts to form a grammatically correct and meaningful sentence.
(P) who had lost their documents in the flood
(Q) the bank opened a special help desk
(R) for customers
(S) and asked them to submit simple self-declarations
questions.explanation: 'The bank opened a special help desk for customers who had lost their documents in the flood and asked them to submit simple self-declarations' = QRPS. In QSRP 'them' would have no antecedent.

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error. If there is no error, choose 'E'.
Of the two proposals, (A)/ the second is the best (B)/ because it requires (C)/ less capital. (D)/ No error (E)
questions.explanation: When two things are compared, the comparative is used: 'the second is the better'. The error is in part B.

questions.question: Which of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT?
options: No sooner had the bell rung than the students rushed out.
Hardly had she reached the station when the train left.
The furniture in the new office are very expensive.
He is one of those officers who never take bribes.
Neither the manager nor the clerks were present at the meeting.
questions.explanation: 'Furniture' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb: 'The furniture … is very expensive'. The other sentences are correct (with 'neither … nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'clerks').

questions.question:
Choose the pair of words that best fills both blanks.
Although the company reported record profits, its shares ______ because investors were ______ about future demand.
questions.explanation: 'Although' signals that the share price moved against the good news: shares fell because investors were worried. Every other pair is internally contradictory or removes the contrast.

questions.question:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The new chairman is known for his ______ approach, preferring careful analysis to hasty decisions.
questions.explanation: Someone who prefers careful analysis to hasty decisions has a 'measured' approach; the other words mean the opposite.

questions.question:
Which pair of the highlighted words should be interchanged to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct?
The (A) announcement by the (B) regulator reassured (C) investors that their (D) deposits were safe.
questions.explanation: The sentence is already meaningful: the regulator's announcement reassured investors that their deposits were safe. Any swap would make it absurd.

questions.question:
In which of the following sentences is the word 'lead' used correctly?
I. The new manager will lead the recovery team.
II. The old water pipes were made of lead.
III. This road leads at the railway station.
questions.explanation: I (verb: to guide) and II (noun: the metal) are correct. In III the verb needs 'to': 'leads to the railway station'.

questions.question:
Choose the option that should replace the phrase in capitals to make the sentence correct.
The board has decided that the new rules WILL COME INTO AFFECT from next month.
questions.explanation: The idiom is 'come into effect' (effect = result/operation, a noun); 'affect' is a verb.

questions.question:
Choose the option that should replace the phrase in capitals to make the sentence correct.
He is used TO WORK late hours during the audit season.
questions.explanation: 'Be used to' (be accustomed to) is followed by a gerund: 'is used to working'.

questions.question:
Match the parts from Column I and Column II to form meaningful sentences.
Column I: (A) Unless the borrower repays on time, (B) Since the policy rate was cut, (C) Although the branch opened late,
Column II: (D) home-loan EMIs have become cheaper. (E) all customers were served before closing time. (F) a penalty will be charged.
questions.explanation: Condition → consequence (A-F); cause → effect (B-D); contrast (C-E).

questions.question:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
The project was approved in March; ______, its funding was delayed by six months.
questions.explanation: Approval followed by a delay is a contrast, so 'however' fits. 'Therefore' and 'consequently' imply cause; 'moreover' and 'similarly' imply addition.

questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to OBSTINATE.
questions.explanation: Obstinate means refusing to change one's opinion — stubborn. 'Flexible' is its opposite.

questions.question: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to SCARCE.
questions.explanation: Scarce means insufficient; its opposite is abundant. The other words are synonyms of scarce.

The table shows the number of electric vehicles sold (in hundreds) by five companies in 2024 and the percentage increase in their sales in 2025 over 2024.
Company | Sales 2024 | % increase in 2025
A | 240 | 25%
B | 180 | 40%
C | 320 | 15%
D | 150 | 60%
E | 280 | 10%

The sales of company D in 2025 are what percent more than the sales of company B in 2024?

A | 240 | 25%

What is the ratio of the sales of company B in 2025 to the sales of company E in 2025?

Company | Sales 2024 | % increase in 2025

What is the difference between the total sales of companies C and E in 2025 and the total sales of companies A and D in 2025?
questions.explanation: C + E (2025) = 368 + 308 = 676 hundred; A + D (2025) = 300 + 240 = 540 hundred. Difference = 136 hundred = 13,600.

questions.question:
A bank's total loan book of ₹7,200 crore is distributed among sectors as follows: Housing 30%, MSME 20%, Agriculture 15%, Education 10%, Vehicle 12.5% and Others 12.5%.

If the distribution is shown in a pie chart, what is the central angle of the Agriculture sector?

A bank's total loan book of ₹7,200 crore is distributed among sectors as follows: Housing 30%, MSME 20%, Agriculture 15%, Education 10%, Vehicle 12.5% and Others 12.5%.

By how much do Housing loans exceed the combined Education and Vehicle loans?
questions.explanation: Housing = 30%; Education + Vehicle = 22.5%. Difference = 7.5% of 7,200 = ₹540 crore.

questions.question:
A bank's total loan book of ₹7,200 crore is distributed among sectors as follows: Housing 30%, MSME 20%, Agriculture 15%, Education 10%, Vehicle 12.5% and Others 12.5%.

If 25% of MSME loans and 10% of Housing loans turn into NPAs, what is the total amount of these NPAs?
questions.explanation: MSME = 1,440 crore → 25% = 360; Housing = 2,160 crore → 10% = 216. Total = ₹576 crore.

questions.question:
Solve and compare.
I. x² − 4x − 21 = 0
II. y² − 10y + 21 = 0
options: x = y or the relationship cannot be established
questions.explanation: I: (x − 7)(x + 3) = 0 → x = 7, −3. II: (y − 3)(y − 7) = 0 → y = 3, 7. x = −3 is less than every y, but x = 7 is greater than y = 3, so no relation can be established.

questions.question:
Compare the quantities.
Quantity I: Speed (in km/h) of a boat in still water, if it covers 36 km downstream in 2 hours and 24 km upstream in 2 hours.
Quantity II: Average of the first 31 natural numbers.
options: Quantity I = Quantity II or the relation cannot be established
questions.explanation: Quantity I: downstream 18 km/h, upstream 12 km/h → still-water speed = (18 + 12)/2 = 15. Quantity II: (1 + 31)/2 = 16. Quantity I < Quantity II.

questions.question: Find the next term: 17, 9, 10, 16.5, 35, ?
Find the wrong number in the series: 8, 12, 21, 38, 62, 98
questions.explanation: Differences should be 2², 3², 4², 5², 6²: 8, 12, 21, 37, 62, 98. 38 should be 37.

questions.question: A shopkeeper allows a discount of 20% on the marked price of an article and still gains 12%. If the marked price is ₹2,100, what is the cost price?

In an election between two candidates, 10% of the voters on the list did not vote and 90 votes cast were invalid. The winner got 54% of the valid votes and won by 324 votes. How many voters were on the list?
questions.explanation: Margin = 54% − 46% = 8% of valid votes = 324 → valid = 4,050. Votes cast = 4,050 + 90 = 4,140 = 90% of the list → 4,600.

questions.question: ₹6,800 is divided among A, B and C such that A gets 2/3 of what B gets and B gets 1/4 of what C gets. What is B's share?

Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 hours and 18 hours respectively, while pipe C can empty it in 24 hours. All three are opened together, and after 4 hours pipe C is closed. In how much more time will the tank be filled?
questions.explanation: Net rate = 1/12 + 1/18 − 1/24 = 7/72; in 4 hours 28/72 is filled. Remaining 44/72 at 10/72 per hour = 4.4 hours = 4 h 24 min.

questions.question: A boat takes 3 hours more to cover 60 km upstream than to cover the same distance downstream. If its speed in still water is 15 km/h, what is the speed of the stream?
₹13,000 is divided into two parts, one lent at 8% and the other at 10% simple interest per annum. The total interest after 2 years is ₹2,320. What is the part lent at 8%?
A committee of 4 is to be formed from 6 men and 4 women. What is the probability that the committee has exactly 2 women?
questions.explanation: Favourable = ⁶C₂ × ⁴C₂ = 15 × 6 = 90; total = ¹⁰C₄ = 210. Probability = 90/210 = 3/7.

questions.question: The radius of a cylinder is increased by 20% and its height is decreased by 20%. What is the percentage change in its volume?
questions.explanation: V ∝ r²h: 1.2² × 0.8 = 1.152, i.e. a 15.2% increase.

questions.question:
Eight persons A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H sit around a circular table. Some of them face the centre and some face away from the centre.
A faces the centre. B sits exactly opposite A and faces the same direction as A. C sits second to the right of B. D sits third to the right of C and faces away from the centre. F sits second to the right of D. E sits immediately to the left of B. H sits second to the right of E. The immediate neighbours of D face opposite directions. H faces the same direction as F, while C faces the direction opposite to F. E and C face the same direction. F does not face the centre.

How many persons face the centre?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from A: A (centre), F (away), C (centre), H (away), B (centre), E (centre), G (away), D (away). A, C, B and E face the centre — four persons.

questions.question:
Eight persons A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H sit around a circular table. Some of them face the centre and some face away from the centre.
A faces the centre. B sits exactly opposite A and faces the same direction as A. C sits second to the right of B. D sits third to the right of C and faces away from the centre. F sits second to the right of D. E sits immediately to the left of B. H sits second to the right of E. The immediate neighbours of D face opposite directions. H faces the same direction as F, while C faces the direction opposite to F. E and C face the same direction. F does not face the centre.

Who sits second to the left of H?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from A: A (centre), F (away), C (centre), H (away), B (centre), E (centre), G (away), D (away). H faces away from the centre, so its left is anticlockwise: second to the left of H is F.

questions.question:
Eight persons A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H sit around a circular table. Some of them face the centre and some face away from the centre.
A faces the centre. B sits exactly opposite A and faces the same direction as A. C sits second to the right of B. D sits third to the right of C and faces away from the centre. F sits second to the right of D. E sits immediately to the left of B. H sits second to the right of E. The immediate neighbours of D face opposite directions. H faces the same direction as F, while C faces the direction opposite to F. E and C face the same direction. F does not face the centre.

Who sits immediately to the right of G?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from A: A (centre), F (away), C (centre), H (away), B (centre), E (centre), G (away), D (away). G faces away from the centre, so its right is clockwise: D.

questions.question:
Eight persons A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H sit around a circular table. Some of them face the centre and some face away from the centre.
A faces the centre. B sits exactly opposite A and faces the same direction as A. C sits second to the right of B. D sits third to the right of C and faces away from the centre. F sits second to the right of D. E sits immediately to the left of B. H sits second to the right of E. The immediate neighbours of D face opposite directions. H faces the same direction as F, while C faces the direction opposite to F. E and C face the same direction. F does not face the centre.

What is the position of E with respect to D?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from A: A (centre), F (away), C (centre), H (away), B (centre), E (centre), G (away), D (away). D faces away from the centre, so its left is anticlockwise: G is immediately to D's left and E second to the left.

questions.question:
Seven persons J, K, L, M, N, O and P live on seven different floors of a building (floor 1 is the lowest and floor 7 the topmost). Each owns a car of a different colour — Red, Blue, Black, White, Grey, Silver and Green.
J lives on an even-numbered floor but not on floor 2. The owner of the Black car lives above J, and only one person lives between them. Only two persons live between L and the owner of the Black car. M lives immediately above the owner of the Black car. K lives on an odd-numbered floor below L. The owner of the Green car lives immediately below J. O lives immediately above P. M owns neither the Red nor the Blue car. The owner of the Silver car lives immediately above the owner of the Blue car. K does not own the Blue car. The owner of the Grey car lives on an even-numbered floor.

Who owns the Silver car?
questions.explanation: Floor 1 to 7: K (Red), N (Grey), L (Green), J (Blue), P (Silver), O (Black), M (White). P owns the Silver car.

questions.question:
Seven persons Q, R, S, T, U, V and W visit seven different cities — Agra, Bhopal, Chennai, Delhi, Indore, Jaipur and Kochi — on seven different days of the same week, from Monday to Sunday (one person each day).
Only two persons make their visits before Q. W visits immediately before Q. The person who visits Jaipur visits immediately after Q. Only two persons visit between the person who visits Jaipur and S, and S visits after T. R visits Chennai. Only one person visits between R and T, and R visits after V. T visits Jaipur. U does not visit on Monday. The person who visits Delhi visits on Monday. The person who visits Kochi visits immediately after the person who visits Delhi. The person who visits Indore visits immediately before the person who visits Chennai. S does not visit Agra.

Who visits Indore?
questions.explanation: Mon – V (Delhi), Tue – W (Kochi), Wed – Q (Agra), Thu – T (Jaipur), Fri – U (Indore), Sat – R (Chennai), Sun – S (Bhopal). U visits Indore.

questions.question:
Statements: Some coins are notes. No note is a cheque. All cheques are drafts.
Conclusions: I. Some drafts are not notes. II. Some coins are not cheques.
questions.explanation: The drafts that are cheques cannot be notes, so I follows. The coins that are notes cannot be cheques, so II follows. Both follow.

questions.question:
Statements: Only a few laptops are tablets. No tablet is a phone.
Conclusions: I. Some laptops are not phones. II. All laptops can be phones.
questions.explanation: The laptops that are tablets cannot be phones, so I follows. For the same reason not all laptops can be phones, so II does not follow.

questions.question:
Statements: R > S ≥ T; U ≤ T < V; W ≥ V
Conclusions: I. W > U  II. S ≥ U
questions.explanation: W ≥ V > T ≥ U gives W > U. S ≥ T ≥ U gives S ≥ U. Both follow.

questions.question:
Statements: J ≤ K < L; M ≥ L; N > M
Conclusions: I. K > N  II. J ≥ L
questions.explanation: N > M ≥ L > K, so K < N and I is false. J ≤ K < L, so J < L and II is false. Neither follows.

questions.question: In a family, M is the only son of N. O is the wife of M. P is the daughter of M and O. Q is the mother of N. R is the husband of N. How is P related to Q?
questions.explanation: N (a woman, since R is her husband) is P's grandmother. Q is N's mother, so P is Q's great-granddaughter.

questions.question: Point A is 7 m north of point B. Point C is 6 m west of B. Point D is 8 m south of C. Point E is 14 m east of D. What is the distance between A and E, and in which direction is E with respect to A?
questions.explanation: With B = (0, 0): A = (0, 7), E = (−6 + 14, −8) = (8, −8). E is 8 m east and 15 m south of A: distance √(64 + 225) = 17 m, towards the South-East.

questions.question: In a certain code, each letter of a word is replaced by the letter in the same position from the other end of the English alphabet (A ↔ Z, B ↔ Y, …). If 'LOAN' is written as 'OLZM', how is 'BOND' written?
questions.explanation: Opposite letters: B → Y, O → L, N → M, D → W. So BOND → YLMW.

questions.question: How many meaningful English words can be formed using all the letters E, I, L and M exactly once each?
questions.explanation: LIME and MILE can be formed — two words.
